title: Graph compactification of a summable series of ordered jumps
statement:
Work in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $V$ be a nonempty compact Hausdorff metrizable totally disconnected space, where totally disconnected means that every connected subset has at most one point. Let $c:V\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and injective, and let $(v_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be pairwise distinct points. Put $D=\{v_k:k\in\mathbb N\}$ and $A=V\setminus D$. Assume $A$ is dense in $V$ and, for every $k$, there are sequences $(x_m^-),(x_m^+)$ in $A$ tending to $v_k$ with $c(x_m^-)<c(v_k)<c(x_m^+)$ for all $m$. Set $a_k=2^{-k-3}$ and, for $x\ne v_k$, set $h_k(x)=-a_k$ if $c(x)<c(v_k)$ and $h_k(x)=a_k$ if $c(x)>c(v_k)$. Define
$$f(x)=\sum_{k\ge0}h_k(x)\quad(x\in A),\qquad g_k=\sum_{j\ne k}h_j(v_k).$$
These series converge absolutely, the series defining $f$ converges uniformly on $A$, $|f(x)|\le1/4$, and $f:A\to[-1/4,1/4]$ is continuous. For every sequence $(x_m)$ in $A$ tending to $v_k$, if $c(x_m)<c(v_k)$ for all $m$, then $f(x_m)\to g_k-a_k$; if $c(x_m)>c(v_k)$ for all $m$, then $f(x_m)\to g_k+a_k$. Let $T$ be the closure of $\Gamma=\{(x,f(x)):x\in A\}$ in $V\times[-1/4,1/4]$, with its subspace topology. Then $T$ is nonempty compact Hausdorff, metrizable and totally disconnected. The first projection $q:T\to V$ is continuous and surjective. For $x\in A$ its fibre is exactly $\{(x,f(x))\}$. For each $k$, its fibre is exactly the two distinct points
$$t_k^-=(v_k,g_k-a_k),\qquad t_k^+=(v_k,g_k+a_k).$$
The graph $\Gamma$ is dense in $T$.

proof.text: Write $b_N=2^{-N-2}$. The finite geometric identity gives $\sum_{j<N}a_j=(1-2^{-N})/4$ and $\sum_{N\le j<M}a_j\le b_N$ for every $M\ge N$. Hence the nonnegative series has sum $1/4$ and tail sum $b_N$, using [lem-wf-real-geometric-summability] with ratio $1/2$ and multiplying by $1/8$. For every $x\in A$, $|h_j(x)|=a_j$; for $j\ne k$, injectivity of $c$ and distinctness of the $v_j$ give $|h_j(v_k)|=a_j$. Thus the absolute-value series converge. Every partial sum, and then every limit, has absolute value at most $1/4$. Deleting one term has the same tail bound.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated topology auxiliary; Step 1: geometric majorant and absolute convergence

proof.text: On $A$, each $h_j$ is locally constant: at $x\in A$ the nonzero real difference $c(x)-c(v_j)$ retains its sign on a neighbourhood by continuity of $c$. Apply [lem-wf-dominated-continuous-function-series] with $K=\mathbb R$, $X=S=A$, $u_j=a_j$, and these continuous $h_j$. The usual real absolute value is multiplicative and its metric is complete, and Step 1 gives the summable majorant. This gives uniform convergence and continuity of $f$ as a real-valued map. The bound from Step 1 lets it corestrict continuously to $[-1/4,1/4]$ by the definition of subspace topology.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated topology auxiliary; Step 2: uniform convergence and continuity on the nonsplit locus

proof.text:
Fix $k$ and put $B_k=A\cup\{v_k\}$. On this space define $u_k=0$ and $u_j=h_j|_{B_k}$ for $j
e k$. These terms are defined everywhere on $B_k$: no $v_j$ for $j
e k$ lies there. Each is locally constant by exactly the sign-neighbourhood argument in Step 2, including at $v_k$, since $c(v_k)
e c(v_j)$. Their norms are bounded by $a_j$. Apply [lem-wf-dominated-continuous-function-series] on $X=S=B_k$ to obtain a continuous sum $G_k$. At $v_k$ it equals $g_k$, and on $A$ the finite-sum identity followed by limits gives $f=G_k+h_k$. A sequence in $A$ converging to $v_k$ also converges in $B_k$. On either prescribed side its $h_k$ value is constantly $-a_k$ or $a_k$, respectively. Continuity of $G_k$ proves exactly the two asserted limits.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated topology auxiliary; Step 3: deleted-term extension and the two side limits

proof.text: Put $I=[-1/4,1/4]$ and $P=V\times I$. By [lem-sfb-real-closed-interval-compact], $I$ is compact. By [lem-weil-pbc-tychonoff-product-quasi-compact], so is $P$. Its closed subset $T=\overline\Gamma$ is compact by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-in-quasi-compact]. Choose a compatible metric $d$ on $V$; $\max(d(x,x^\prime),|y-y^\prime|)$ is a compatible metric on $P$, whose restriction metrizes $T$ (its balls are products of balls in the factors). Hausdorffness follows from the metrics. Since $A$ is dense in nonempty $V$, $A$ and $\Gamma$ are nonempty, and hence $T$ is nonempty. Projection $q$ is continuous by the product and subspace topologies. Finally $\Gamma$ is dense in its closure $T$ by the definition of closure.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated topology auxiliary; Step 4: compact Hausdorff metrizable graph closure

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-continuous-image-quasi-compact], $q(T)$ is compact. Since $V$ is Hausdorff, [lem-sfb-compact-subset-hausdorff-closed] makes $q(T)$ closed. It contains $A=q(\Gamma)$, and density of $A$ therefore gives $q(T)=V$. Thus $q$ is surjective.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated topology auxiliary; Step 5: surjectivity

proof.text: For any $(x,y)\in T$, choose $(x_n,f(x_n))\in\Gamma$ within $1/(n+1)$ of $(x,y)$ in the compatible product metric; these exist by the definition of closure. Then $x_n\to x$ and $f(x_n)\to y$. If $x\in A$, convergence also holds in the subspace $A$. Continuity from Step 2 implies $f(x_n)\to f(x)$, so uniqueness of real limits gives $y=f(x)$. Conversely $(x,f(x))\in\Gamma\subseteq T$. This proves the claimed singleton fibre.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated topology auxiliary; Step 6: singleton fibres by metric closure and continuity

proof.text: If $x=v_k$, use a graph sequence as in Step 6. Every $x_n\in A$ differs from $v_k$, so injectivity of $c$ puts it on exactly one of the two sides. One of those sides occurs infinitely often; enumerate its indices in increasing order to obtain a subsequence. Step 3 gives its height limit $g_k-a_k$ or $g_k+a_k$, while convergence of the original height sequence gives the same limit $y$. Hence there are no other fibre points. For existence of both points, use the two side sequences supplied in the hypotheses and Step 3. Their graph points converge in $P$ to $(v_k,g_k\mp a_k)$: these real heights lie in $I$ since all approximating heights lie in the closed interval $I$. Every neighbourhood of either limit meets $\Gamma$, so both belong to $T$. Finally their difference is $2a_k>0$, proving distinctness.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated topology auxiliary; Step 7: exact double fibres, including existence of both limits

proof.text: Let $C\subseteq T$ be connected. Its image $q(C)$ is connected: a separation of the image by relatively open sets would pull back under $q$ to a separation of $C$. Total disconnectedness of $V$ says $q(C)$ has at most one point. If $C$ is nonempty it is therefore contained in one fibre. By Steps 6–7 that fibre has at most two points. A two-point subset of the metric space $T$ is discrete (use disjoint balls of radius less than half their positive distance); if $C$ contained both, these singleton opens would separate it. Thus $C$ has at most one point, also when empty. This is precisely total disconnectedness of $T$.

I also read the full statements of the 7 cited nodes and of def-weil-size-convention, and parent Steps 2-4. The statement is unchanged against the earlier Q117 snapshots and matches what the parent uses. Steps 1-3: the sum of a_k=2^{-k-3} is 1/4. The h_j are locally constant on A, by injectivity of c and distinctness of the v_k. The dominated-series leaf applies on A to give uniform convergence and continuity of f. On B_k=A∪{v_k}, with the k-th term set to 0, it gives a continuous G_k with G_k(v_k)=g_k and f=G_k+h_k, so the side limits are g_k∓a_k. The proof never claims that f extends across a jump. Steps 4-5: I compact (new leaf), then the Tychonoff, closed-subset, compact-image and compact-in-Hausdorff-is-closed leaves give compact T and surjective q. The max metric gives metrizability. Steps 6-8 are elementary and correct: the fibre over A is a singleton by continuity of f, and the fibre over v_k is exactly {g_k±a_k}. Existence comes from the side-sequence hypotheses, and the heights lie in I because I is closed. T is totally disconnected because its fibres are finite and V is totally disconnected. Edge cases checked: k=0, N=0, A nonempty from density, isolated or extreme v_k excluded by the hypothesis.
